item.text: {"facts":[{"source_id":"SRC-4cc9fecc20173873","start_unit":5,"end_unit":6,"fact_summary":"In April 2023, the Supreme Court struck down the 2022 transfer of the National Guard’s organic, administrative, budgetary, and managerial control from the civilian Security Ministry to the Defense Ministry, holding that the Guard was constitutionally civilian; López Obrador had supported the transfer, argued military control was necessary to prevent corruption and ensure professionalism, and criticized the justices as politically biased.","question_ids":["3B.2","3B.4","4B.4","4B.10","8B.2","8B.6","8B.8","8B.9"],"polarity":"mixed","period_fit":"The ruling and presidential response occurred in 2023; the challenged legislation was enacted in 2022 and the Guard was established in 2019.","ruler_attribution":"The article attributes the transfer policy and public criticism of the Court to López Obrador and his administration.","limitations":["The document does not establish the final extent of administrative compliance after the ruling.","It reports allegations and official positions without independently resolving whether military control improved professionalism or reduced corruption."]},{"source_id":"SRC-4cc9fecc20173873","start_unit":6,"end_unit":6,"fact_summary":"The administration relied heavily on the armed forces for public security, infrastructure construction, customs, and ports; approximately 130,000 National Guard troops and tens of thousands of soldiers and marines performed public-security tasks, while violent crime remained a major problem and National Guard members faced criminal investigations over alleged killings, including the deaths of two people in Nuevo Laredo.","question_ids":["3B.2","3B.6","3B.9","3B.10","4B.5","8B.3","8B.6","8B.7","8B.9","8B.10"],"polarity":"mixed","period_fit":"The article was published in 2023 and describes the administration’s ongoing deployment and reported incidents around that period.","ruler_attribution":"The article directly attributes the expanded military role and deployment policy to López Obrador.","limitations":["The source gives no complete causal evaluation of homicide trends or the administration’s alternative welfare programs.","The reported Nuevo Laredo allegations were described as under investigation rather than adjudicated."]},{"source_id":"SRC-99d0b68393d8ab87","start_unit":2,"end_unit":3,"fact_summary":"Mexico’s specialized electoral prosecutor closed a two-year investigation into Pío López Obrador, after videos showed him receiving approximately one million pesos in cash from David León in 2015 for Morena-related campaign activity; prosecutors concluded the conduct did not constitute an electoral crime, but the decision still required federal judicial confirmation. López Obrador offered to testify to the FGR, but had not done so by the time reported.","question_ids":["4B.2","4B.4","7B.3","7B.4","7B.6","7B.7","7B.9","7B.10"],"polarity":"mixed","period_fit":"The source concerns a 2022 prosecutorial decision and earlier conduct, not a 2023 event, but is relevant to the ruler’s integrity and accountability context in 2023.","ruler_attribution":"The article reports the president’s family relationship, his offer to testify, and the institutional handling of the investigation; it does not establish that López Obrador directed the prosecutorial decision.","limitations":["The source does not establish that the money was illegal or that López Obrador personally benefited.","The account predates 2023 and reports a pending judicial confirmation."]},{"source_id":"SRC-b3c3415aecb75c03","start_unit":1,"end_unit":5,"fact_summary":"A 2024 retrospective by MCCI described potential conflicts involving López Obrador’s family and associates: a son’s residence linked to a Baker Hughes executive while the company held Pemex contracts; contracts and public purchases allegedly directed to friends of another son; large health-supply contracts to a company with regulatory problems; benefits connected to Dos Bocas, Tren Maya, and Sembrando Vida; contracts to a presidential cousin; and alleged nepotistic or inexperienced appointments. The article also states that López Obrador issued a 2019 memorandum rejecting family business with government, but concludes that the reported cases were not consistently remedied and that his son later became a party official.","question_ids":["5B.5","5B.6","5B.7","7B.3","7B.4","7B.5","7B.6","7B.7","7B.8","7B.9","7B.10","8B.2","8B.4","8B.6","8B.8","8B.10"],"polarity":"adverse","period_fit":"The document was published in 2024 and includes incidents from 2019–2023, including several developments reported during 2023; it is retrospective rather than a contemporaneous 2023 report.","ruler_attribution":"The article attributes the memorandum and the administration’s appointments and contracting environment to López Obrador, but reports alleged benefits involving family members, friends, and officials rather than proving presidential personal direction.","limitations":["The source is an advocacy and investigative retrospective, and several claims are presented as potential conflicts or allegations rather than final legal findings.","The article does not provide a complete government response or independent adjudication for every case."]},{"source_id":"SRC-a9bc04d64a8c9007","start_unit":2,"end_unit":4,"fact_summary":"In March 2023, López Obrador acknowledged that the Army used Pegasus but characterized it as lawful intelligence work rather than spying and said intelligence was used to avoid force. Reporting based on Guacamaya documents and forensic findings stated that Sedena had purchased Pegasus in 2019 and remotely monitored journalists and activists investigating military abuses; the administration and Defense Ministry had previously denied the purchase or use, and the president again denied illegal spying while accusing reporting media and NGOs of opposing his government.","question_ids":["3B.3","3B.4","3B.5","3B.8","4B.3","4B.6","4B.9","7B.1","7B.2","7B.6","7B.7","7B.10"],"polarity":"adverse","period_fit":"The presidential statements and reporting occurred in March 2023, while the alleged surveillance began in 2019 and evidence was disclosed through 2022–2023.","ruler_attribution":"The article directly attributes the public defense and characterization of Pegasus use to López Obrador and reports Sedena’s institutional role.","limitations":["The article reports competing official and civil-society interpretations of legality.","It does not establish that López Obrador personally ordered surveillance of specific individuals."]},{"source_id":"SRC-62d5862c36f8cd25","start_unit":2,"end_unit":4,"fact_summary":"Amnesty’s Mexico report described increased militarization of public security, legislation extending armed-forces participation through 2028, excessive National Guard force, and weak transparency and accountability. It reported 476 complaints against the National Guard and 404 against Sedena, killings and arbitrary detention allegations, 9,826 missing-person cases in 2022, only 36 disappearance convictions, interference in the Ayotzinapa investigation, Pegasus monitoring of civil society, and presidential stigmatization of feminists, journalists, and human-rights defenders. It also recorded some institutional or rights developments, including a National Centre for Human Identification, court-ordered forensic database creation, expanded abortion legality, nationwide same-sex marriage, and Supreme Court protections for migrants.","question_ids":["3B.1","3B.2","3B.3","3B.4","3B.5","3B.6","3B.7","3B.8","3B.9","3B.10","4B.3","4B.4","4B.6","4B.7","4B.9","4B.10","6B.3","6B.5","6B.6","6B.8","6B.9","6B.10","7B.2","7B.6","7B.7","8B.2","8B.3","8B.6","8B.8","8B.9","8B.10"],"polarity":"mixed","period_fit":"The report was published in 2023 but primarily covers 2022; it is relevant as the immediately preceding baseline for evaluating López Obrador’s 2023 posture.","ruler_attribution":"The report attributes militarization, legislative initiatives, presidential rhetoric, and government institutional responses to López Obrador’s administration.","limitations":["The report’s principal evidence period is 2022 rather than 2023.","It does not provide a complete assessment of economic policy, international peace, nuclear risk, or administrative effectiveness."]},{"source_id":"SRC-54a79c2b8521887b","start_unit":4,"end_unit":8,"fact_summary":"Human Rights Watch reported that violence reached historic highs under López Obrador, with widespread impunity, torture, disappearances, attacks on journalists and defenders, and expanded military responsibilities in law enforcement, immigration, public works, and social programs. It also reported Pegasus use despite presidential promises, alleged military obstruction of abuse investigations, serious risks to migrants and Indigenous communities, underfunded protection mechanisms, and weak disability and climate protections. Countervailing developments included National Search Commission initiatives, expanded abortion and same-sex-marriage access, ratification of ILO Convention C190, and reforms restricting forced psychiatric treatment and restraints.","question_ids":["3B.1","3B.2","3B.4","3B.5","3B.6","3B.7","3B.8","3B.10","4B.3","4B.4","4B.6","4B.7","4B.9","4B.10","5B.6","5B.7","6B.3","6B.5","6B.6","6B.8","6B.9","6B.10","7B.2","7B.6","7B.7","8B.2","8B.3","8B.4","8B.6","8B.8","8B.9","8B.10"],"polarity":"mixed","period_fit":"The report was published for events of 2022 and therefore supplies recent baseline and institutional context for 2023, not a full 2023 measurement.","ruler_attribution":"The report directly attributes expanded military responsibilities, immigration enforcement, climate and infrastructure policies, and several reforms to the López Obrador administration.","limitations":["Most quantitative indicators concern 2021–2022 rather than 2023.","The report does not cover nuclear risk, conventional interstate conflict, or detailed macroeconomic performance."]},{"source_id":"SRC-f58e5dc886bda2e2","start_unit":3,"end_unit":15,"fact_summary":"Freedom House characterized Mexico as partly free, with routine electoral alternation and generally competitive multiparty elections, but severe rule-of-law deficits, corruption, violence, impunity, attacks on critics, and risks to journalists. It reported presidential attacks on media, civil society, autonomous institutions, and election bodies; concerns about military politicization and transparency; weak anti-corruption enforcement; limited judicial independence and due process; excessive force against protesters; and discrimination and insecurity affecting Indigenous people, migrants, women, LGBT+ people, and people with disabilities. It also noted some favorable developments, including competitive opposition gains, women’s political representation, legal protections, increased redistributive spending and minimum wages, labor reforms, and legal expansion for abortion, same-sex marriage, and gender recognition.","question_ids":["3B.1","3B.2","3B.3","3B.4","3B.5","3B.6","3B.7","3B.8","3B.10","4B.1","4B.2","4B.3","4B.4","4B.5","4B.6","4B.7","4B.8","4B.9","4B.10","5B.1","5B.4","5B.5","5B.6","5B.7","5B.8","5B.10","6B.1","6B.2","6B.3","6B.4","6B.5","6B.8","6B.9","6B.10","7B.1","7B.2","7B.5","7B.6","7B.7","7B.8","7B.9","7B.10","8B.1","8B.2","8B.3","8B.4","8B.5","8B.6","8B.7","8B.8","8B.9","8B.10"],"polarity":"mixed","period_fit":"The report covers 2021 and was published as the 2022 country report; it is contextual baseline evidence for 2023 rather than direct 2023 evidence.","ruler_attribution":"The report attributes presidential rhetoric, military expansion, legislative actions, appointments, and administration policies to López Obrador or his government.","limitations":["The source does not provide direct 2023 outcomes for most indicators.","It contains aggregate country assessments that cannot always isolate presidential causation."]},{"source_id":"SRC-afa81f3662511290","start_unit":60,"end_unit":61,"fact_summary":"In January 2023, Mexico’s Supreme Court ruled that soldiers could arrest people without first notifying civilian police, provided the arrest was eventually registered in a civilian-accessible computer system. The ruling followed López Obrador’s support for continued and expanded military law-enforcement responsibilities; critics argued that militarization weakened separation of powers, while the article noted police capacity constraints and concerns that military and National Guard personnel lacked proper arrest and investigative training.","question_ids":["3B.1","3B.2","3B.4","3B.5","3B.6","3B.10","4B.4","4B.9","8B.2","8B.5","8B.6","8B.9"],"polarity":"mixed","period_fit":"The Supreme Court ruling and reported presidential policy occurred in January 2023.","ruler_attribution":"The article directly attributes support for indefinite military reliance and expanded military responsibilities to López Obrador.","limitations":["The article does not establish whether the registration requirement was implemented effectively or whether arrests increased or decreased harm.","It reports critics’ concerns and police-capacity arguments without a full legal or outcome evaluation."]},{"source_id":"SRC-5a57755b9ffcd405","start_unit":60,"end_unit":61,"fact_summary":"In February 2023, activist Raymundo Ramos said the Army and government were linking him to a drug cartel after he investigated military killings and publicly denounced the deaths of five young men in Nuevo Laredo. A president-selected questioner used López Obrador’s morning press briefing to air the cartel accusation; Ramos denied it, prior Pegasus surveillance of his phone had been confirmed by Citizen Lab, and available crime-scene and Army reports did not list the weapons asserted by the questioner.","question_ids":["3B.3","3B.4","3B.8","3B.9","4B.3","4B.6","4B.9","7B.1","7B.2","7B.6","7B.7","7B.10","8B.9"],"polarity":"adverse","period_fit":"The reported incident and presidential press briefing occurred in February 2023; the Pegasus intrusion dated to 2020.","ruler_attribution":"The article attributes the press-briefing format and questioner selection to López Obrador and reports alleged Army involvement; it does not establish that the president ordered the smear or surveillance.","limitations":["The alleged government role is based partly on Ramos’s suspicion and contextual evidence.","The article does not report a final investigation or judicial finding about the killings or the accusation."]}],"documents_with_no_material_fact":["SRC-3f8f8f20305d5fe8","SRC-450effe68974c2c2","SRC-4605cdc31a8213f9"],"batch_limitations":["The supplied corpus is heavily concentrated on human rights, militarization, political freedom, and integrity; it contains little or no direct evidence on nuclear risk, interstate peace, macroeconomic policy, social-service delivery, or comprehensive 2023 outcomes.","Several supplied reports cover 2021 or 2022 and therefore function as baseline or context for 2023 rather than direct 2023 evidence.","The AP document SRC-afa81f3662511290 contains extensive page-navigation material, but only units 60–61 contain the substantive article."]}
